refreshes.scope: Platform, deployment and reliability under PenniLogic/docs#27: infrastructure as code, environments, deploy pipelines, the feature-flag and kill-switch mechanism, residency policy and the database extension gate (infra#25); backups, point-in-time recovery and the restore drill (infra#26); traces, metrics, logs, SLOs, alert routing, on-call, clock synchronisation and in-region tamper-evident log retention (infra#27); governed human access to production data stores, backups and keys (infra#32); backend log scrubbing and the no-financial-data-in-logs gate (api#21); the notification and transactional email outbox with providers, delivery callbacks and sessionless unsubscribe (api#56); the Android and web notification preference editors (android#56, web#21); Play App Signing, the AAB pipeline, tracks and staged rollout (android#37). data_flows.erasure_path: Live erasure destroys the user's DEK, IK and AK and physically clears platform-key values (ADR-018 section 6.7). Backups are not cleaned by that: until the infra#26 retention bound, backups and secondary-region copies still hold the wrapped keys and ciphertext (recoverable by a party with the backup key and custodian unwrap rights on that KEK version), contact channels and push tokens under platform keys, and, per ADR-021, pre-redaction group ciphertext with the still-live group key and pre-pseudonymisation viewer and user identifiers readable with the backup alone. A restore replays the key journal and the infra#33 tombstones before readiness (ADR-018 section 6.6); multi-subject copies (split seats, group-key ciphertext, access-event viewer identifiers) and derived copies follow the ADR-021 placeholder and pseudonymisation steps, which the T-SEC-07 replay repeats. During the window the controls are backup-key and KEK-custodian separation (E24-F13) and backup access separation (infra#26, infra#32); E24-F07 covers resurrection on restore.

categories.analysis: Parties that must prove identity: the deploy pipeline towards the runtime hosts, secret store and key custodian (infra#25), the Android release pipeline and its Play publishing service account (android#37), push and e-mail providers calling back into the API (api#56), anonymous holders of an unsubscribe reference, and operators opening brokered sessions (infra#32). None of these controls exists today: every child ticket is open and the R4 runtime of ADR-022 is a future target. The trust root that matters most is the pipeline's federated credential: infra#25 requires short-lived federated credentials and no long-lived cloud keys but does not state which workflow, branch and environment claims the trust policy binds, so a pull-request or fork workflow that can mint the same token could deploy (E24-F01). Forged provider callbacks and guessed unsubscribe references are reviewed under request_forgery (E24-F15, E24-F16); the Play Console reset route under administrative identity (E24-F17). Upload-key custody, which E25 delegated to this refresh: android#37 owns custody, rotation and recovery and short-lived federated pipeline credentials, but does not say that the upload key and the Play publishing credential are reachable only from the protected release workflow and environment, so a feature-branch or pull-request workflow in the Android repository could sign or publish a malicious bundle, and no rotation drill is recorded (E24-F24). The organisation itself must prove its origin: whoever controls the registrar and DNS account, certificate issuance or a host's TLS private key can serve the genuine origin, relay passkey assertions or alter the assetlinks and webauthn files that ADR-019 places on the relying-party apex, where a wrong RP ID is unfixable once credentials exist; ADR-022 selects self-managed hosts with no managed edge, android#27 owns client certificate pinning whose rotation must follow server key changes, and no existing ticket covered domain, DNS, certificate or TLS-key custody; infra#95 now owns it (E24-F20). The parser-config signing chain is outside this epic: android#37 signs the application bundle only, and no E24 ticket distributes remotely updatable parser rules (docs#51 owns the template runbook).
evidence: PenniLogic/infra#25: short-lived federated pipeline credentials, no deploy from a developer machine
PenniLogic/android#37: Play App Signing custody and short-lived federated pipeline credentials
ADR-022: R4 runtime is a future target; no production credential is authorised
ADR-019: RP ID unfixable once credentials exist; assetlinks and webauthn files served from the RP ID apex (android#20, web#8, infra)
governance/threat-model/records/E25.json: upload-key custody, rotation and recovery delegated to the E24 refresh (android#37)

categories.analysis: Modifiable assets: infrastructure definitions and their applied state, deployable images and the Android bundle, the feature-flag and kill-switch store that infra#25 makes changeable without a deploy (ADR-022 puts the AI kill switch in a primary-database flag store whose ON transition needs two operators), the template payload allowlist (api#56), backups and point-in-time logs (infra#26) and the retained security logs (infra#27). Planned detection: drift detection and pipeline-only deploys (infra#25), the reproducible-build check and track gate (android#37), the ledger zero-sum check on restored data (infra#26), append-only retention with deletion refused (infra#27), which stops deletion but not forged or injected entries (E24-F23) and artifact provenance verification (infra#31, E25). Gaps: no ticket says who may change a flag or kill switch outside the two-operator AI path, how such a change is authorised and recorded, or that a flag can never grant an entitlement or bypass a quota or egress check (E24-F02); and a restore is verified only against the ledger, not against backup checksums or the ADR-020 audit chain and its write-once copy, so a tampered or partial backup could be served (E24-F03). Host packages, kernel, Docker Engine and nftables on the R4 hosts can be altered or left vulnerable outside the IaC drift check; that is reviewed under elevation_of_privilege (E24-F22). Ingestion boundary: the server stores only structured fields (ADR-004), so backups and logs hold no raw message text by construction. Parser-config signing: no E24 ticket ships parser rules; android#37 signs only the application bundle (see spoofing).
evidence: ADR-022: kill switch store, seeded OFF, ON requires two independent eligible operators (adr/ai-egress-consequences.json kill_switch)
ADR-020: section 8.5 chain verification against the write-once copy
PenniLogic/infra#26: ledger zero-sum check and sample reconciliation on restored data
PenniLogic/infra#31: artifact and IaC supply-chain verification (E25)

categories.analysis: Actions that must be attributable later: deployments, canary aborts, rollbacks, flag and kill-switch changes, IaC applies (infra#25), restore drills and restores (infra#26), Play track promotions and rollout halts (android#37), brokered production reads and their approvals (infra#32), alert acknowledgements (infra#27) and preference or unsubscribe changes (api#56). infra#32 already requires statement, object and key-use audit with actor and approval reference, projected into the ADR-020 streams, and infra#27 owns clock synchronisation and in-region append-only retention for CERT-In (O-9), with the period read from the docs#44 profile. infra#25 publishes deploy start, finish, canary verdict and rollback events with duration and version but not the approving principal, nor flag changes, so a production change made under the single owner account cannot later be tied to the session and approval that authorised it (E24-F04). The retained CERT-In logs are only as trustworthy as their time and their writers: ADR-020 section 8.5 requires every host that writes or verifies a stream to use the jurisdiction profile's time source, and DPoP freshness under ADR-019 depends on server time, yet infra#27 measures drift only against the configured source, so a spoofed or shifted source goes unnoticed; and nothing authenticates emitters to the collector or separates client telemetry from security logs, so a compromised or unauthenticated emitter can inject or forge entries that append-only retention then preserves (E24-F23). The single-account procedural separation itself is accepted in governance/DELIVERY.md and not re-opened here.
evidence: PenniLogic/infra#32: broker audit with actor, approval reference and row or object count
PenniLogic/infra#27: clock drift alerting and in-region append-only security-log retention
governance/DELIVERY.md: one account, procedural not cryptographic separation
ADR-020: section 8.5 hosts writing or verifying a stream use the jurisdiction profile's time source; occurred_at regression is a finding

categories.analysis: Data classes are the six data_flows entries: backups, telemetry, messaging data, preference edits, operator access records and client traffic at the public ingress. Ingestion boundary: E24 sits wholly on the structured side; no E24 path carries captured message, notification or statement content (ADR-004). Leak paths: log, trace and metric sinks; alert and page payloads; hosted telemetry, crash, push, e-mail and paging processors possibly outside India; restored or lower-environment copies; notification previews. Planned controls: api#21 scrubs the api backend's logs fail-closed with a static rule and a planted-value runtime scan; api#56 restricts templates to a payload allowlist excluding amounts, merchants and other users; infra#26 refuses unscrubbed restores into lower environments; infra#25 enforces a residency policy for stateful resources; android#18 (E27) owns crash-report scrubbing on the device. Gaps: api#21 covers one service's logs, while traces, span attributes and metric labels from every service (ai-service, admin API) reach the collector with no filter of their own (E24-F05); infra#25's residency policy covers stateful resources, not hosted server telemetry or paging processors, and alert payloads can copy log excerpts to them (E24-F06); the Android crash SDK is a client-embedded processor that android#18 inventories and docs#44 must cover with an agreement and transfer basis, not something an infra policy check can enforce; a pre-erasure backup can resurrect an erased user (E24-F07); provider-side copies of addresses and tokens survive account erasure (E24-F08). Raw content never leaves the device: no E24 server path can receive it (ADR-004); the client paths are crash reports and Android logs, which android#18 and the traffic capture of android#16 must prove clean, and android#37 configures the crash reporter and mapping upload and requires that no financial value and no message content reaches the crash reporter.
evidence: PenniLogic/api#21: structured logging, fail-closed scrubber and planted-value gate
PenniLogic/api#56: template payload allowlist checked at build time
PenniLogic/android#18: error-report scrubbing with a planted monetary value (E27)
ADR-004: the server API has no field for raw message content
PenniLogic/android#37: crash reports configured so no financial value and no message content reaches the crash reporter

categories.analysis: Exhaustible resources: request capacity of the public ingress on self-managed hosts, which ADR-022 section 3.3 makes a platform obligation while the baseline perimeter (architecture/02-security-architecture.md: WAF, rate limiter and DDoS protection) assumed a managed edge; provider sending quotas and spend for push and e-mail, the outbox queue and its dead-letter replays (api#56), telemetry ingestion and the append-only retained log store that cannot be purged before expiry (infra#27), on-call attention, backup storage, and the anonymous unsubscribe path. Planned bounds: api#56 has backoff, retry limits and a dead-letter queue; infra#27 rolls back a noisy alert rule; android#37 halts a staged rollout automatically on a Vitals breach; load and chaos suites, including webhook storms, belong to infra#29 (E25). Gaps: no per-recipient or per-class send cap, no priority that keeps security messages flowing during a flood, and no handling of a provider throttling or suspending the account (E24-F09); no ingestion, cardinality or volume bound protects write-once retained storage, which a log flood fills irreversibly, and no alert de-duplication protects on-call attention (E24-F10); and no existing ticket bounded edge request capacity, per-address and per-route limits or flood absorption for the self-managed ingress (api#40 limits authentication and sensitive operations only), so a request flood takes every service down; infra#96 now owns the ingress capacity plan (E24-F21).
evidence: PenniLogic/api#56: published backoff, retry limit and dead-letter queue
PenniLogic/infra#29: load, stress, soak and chaos suites with webhook storms (E25)
ADR-022: section 3.3 capacity and availability are obligations of the platform tickets; no managed edge

categories.analysis: Capabilities at stake: the deploy identity that applies infrastructure code can rewrite IAM, key policy, retention locks and backup policy, and so grant itself or a human standing access (E24-F11); on the ADR-022 R4 self-managed hosts, shell, container-engine or hypervisor access reads process memory and disks, which infra#32's database, object, backup and key inventory does not name (E24-F12); the production KEK custodian, which ADR-018 section 6.1.1 and ADR-022 section 3.3 assign to T-PLT-03 (infra#27) although infra#27's body does not list it, decides whether a host or account compromise yields every key (baseline T-11, E24-F13). Host vulnerability management is unanalysed by any child: ADR-022 section 3.3 names host patching an obligation of the platform tickets and its section 7 re-runs the enforcement probes after a kernel change, but no ticket sets a patch cadence, a kernel, Docker Engine or runc CVE response, vulnerability and drift scanning of host images or re-qualification of the runtime gates after patching, so a compromised workload can escape to the host and bypass namespaces, nftables and the broker (E24-F22; infra#31 scans IaC and container images and infra#28 application dependencies, not host packages). Planned controls: infra#26 forbids the application role from reading or deleting backups; infra#32 empties standing human grants, enforces FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY inventory and denies CI and workstation access; android#37 limits the Play service account to upload and track management. Preference and device endpoints must reject another user's identifier; api#23 (E25) owns object-authorization tests across the endpoint inventory.
evidence: PenniLogic/infra#32: empty standing-access inventory, CI and workstation denial, FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY check
ADR-018: section 6.1.1 KEK custody requirements, selection by T-PLT-03
PenniLogic/api#23: object-level authorization coverage across the endpoint inventory (E25)

ADR-022: section 3.3 host patching is a platform-ticket obligation; section 7 re-runs probes after a kernel change; T-PLT-01 owns the suite-pass manifest bound to kernel, Docker and nftables configuration

ADR-022: section 11 affected-consumers table maps infra#27 (T-PLT-03) to custodian and observability; adr/ai-egress-consequences.json audit_evidence.custody_owners and delivery.consumers (T-PLT-03 is PenniLogic/infra#27)

categories.analysis: No E24 ticket verifies a purchase, processes a store or payment webhook, or changes a plan or price: api#56's delivery callbacks report message status only, and android#37 excludes pricing configuration and limits the Play service account to upload and track management. Billing verification first appears in E14 (PenniLogic/docs#15) through api#32, whose Definition of Ready refresh reviews this category.

E24 stores no entitlement state, but infra#25 builds a flag and kill-switch mechanism changeable without a deploy. ADR-023 resolves entitlement server-side from plan versions and the usage ledger, so a flag must never become a second entitlement source or switch off a quota reservation; nothing in infra#25 says so, which is part of E24-F02. A point-in-time restore also rewinds the usage ledger to the recovery point; infra#26's sample reconciliation of restored data is where a lost quota or purchase event must be detected, but nothing requires reconciling against an independent record, and a consistent snapshot passes the zero-sum check (E24-F25).
evidence: ADR-023: entitlement resolved server-side from plan versions and the append-only usage ledger
PenniLogic/infra#26: restored data passes the ledger zero-sum check and a sample reconciliation; recovery point objective published

categories.analysis: E24 provides the runtime the AI gateway runs on. ADR-022 names T-PLT-01 (infra#25) as an owner of runtime gates T7 (kill-switch evidence), T12 (self and private address denial at startup), T19 (closed startup and nftables order) and T20 (pipeline digest and deployment-gate enforcement), and T-PLT-02 (infra#26) of T17 (revocation and restore evidence). infra#25 records which primitive satisfies each egress requirement but not that the AI workload stays undeployed until those gates pass, nor that provider keys in the secret store are unreadable to the deploy identity (E24-F14). ADR-022 section 7 forbids hosts, addresses, model names and key-derived values as metric labels; that rule binds infra#27's conventions (E24-F05).
evidence: ADR-022: R4 runtime, gateway-only egress and the 60-second kill-switch bound
PenniLogic/infra#30: network-layer egress denial for the AI workload

categories.analysis: Two E24 entry points accept requests without a user session: the sessionless unsubscribe reference (contracts#15, api#56, reconciled by android#56 and web#21) and provider delivery callbacks (api#56). Neither ticket requires the unsubscribe reference to be unguessable and non-enumerable or the withdrawal to need an explicit confirming request, so a link prefetcher or a guessed reference silences a user's messages (E24-F15); api#56 maps callback statuses but does not authenticate the caller or reject replays, and api#32's verification covers billing providers only (E24-F16). Browser-session forgery against web#21 is bounded by ADR-019: the web access token is DPoP-bound in script memory and the refresh cookie is SameSite=Strict. No E24 ticket fetches a user-supplied URL; alert routes are code.
evidence: PenniLogic/contracts#15: unsubscribe reference scoped to one class and one recipient, single-purpose
ADR-019: web access token held in script memory and DPoP-bound, refresh token in a SameSite=Strict cookie (web#8)

categories.analysis: No E24 ticket passes content to a model or an AI agent: outbox templates take allowlisted fields, logs and traces are scrubbed and are not fed to any model, and preference editors render server state. The AI gateway, tool dispatcher and injection defences belong to E17 (PenniLogic/docs#18) and ai-service#4; delivery sessions reading public comments are governed by PenniLogic/.github#4 (E01-F03).

E24 computes no shares and records no settlement. Split rows are copied by backups like every ledger row. infra#26's planned zero-sum check (open, not a control today) passes on any consistent point-in-time snapshot, so it cannot show that settlements recorded after the recovery point survived or that an erased seat was not resurrected; infra#33 plans a counterparty shared-balance integrity test after restore, so a restore that rewinds settlements recorded after the recovery point (a settled share reappearing as owed) is a split-settlement finding of this epic, carried by E24-F25 (primary category entitlement_tampering, handed to infra#26); share rules, settlements and counterparty erasure belong to E15 (PenniLogic/docs#16) through api#49.

Administrative identities this epic creates or relies on: the hosting account that owns the R4 hosts, networks, backups, secondary region and key custodian; the domain registrar and DNS account that controls the public origin; the Play Console developer account that can add users, promote tracks and request an upload-key reset; the push, e-mail, telemetry, crash and paging service consoles; the on-call roster; and the single basiltt owner account. GitHub owner-account hardening was deferred by owner decision: infra#43 was closed as not planned with an owner-accepted residual risk (phishing-resistant sign-in, per-machine credential verification, rotation and alerting and the revocation drill unfulfilled; organisation 2FA enforcement off; a broadly scoped OAuth credential), so E01-F04 remains an unremediated finding. For E24 this means the E24-F01 trust-policy binding, the protected branch and the production environment approval are only as strong as that account, because the infra#25 deploy pipeline runs as GitHub workflows on GitHub-hosted runners (governance/DELIVERY.md configures only those runners). infra#32 governs human access to data stores, backups and keys with a two-approver roster that fails closed, which in a one-owner organisation means human production-data sessions stay disabled until two eligible approvers exist. Gaps: android#37 documents upload-key custody and who may promote but not Play Console account hardening, the user roster or the upload-key reset path as a compromise route (E24-F17); and no existing ticket owned the console accounts of the push, e-mail and paging or uptime services, whose holders can read recipient lists and delivery history or silence pages during an incident; api#59 covers only the ADR-020 administrative identity domain; infra#93 now owns their governance (E24-F18). The hosting-account owner can snapshot or delete hosts, disks, backups and the secondary region and re-grant itself access, and the registrar and DNS account can repoint the origin; infra#32 inventories standing grants to data stores, not these owner identities, and no existing ticket covered their sign-in, break-glass custody or owner-action alerting; infra#94 now owns their hardening (E24-F19).
evidence: PenniLogic/infra#43: closed as not planned with an owner-accepted residual risk; GitHub owner-account hardening deferred, E01-F04 unremediated
PenniLogic/infra#32: second-approved, time-boxed, brokered human sessions with a fail-closed approver roster
ADR-020: separate administrative identity domain and break-glass rules

findings.title: The deploy pipeline's federated trust policy is not bound to repository, protected branch and environment
findings.attack_path: A pull-request, fork or feature-branch workflow in an infra or service repository requests the same federated token the production deploy job uses; a trust policy that checks only the organisation or repository issues it, and the job deploys an unreviewed image or applies unreviewed infrastructure code to production hosts.
findings.recommended_control: Bind the deploy credential's trust policy to the exact repository, protected main branch and named production environment with required approval; refuse pull-request and fork contexts; keep tokens short-lived; add a negative test proving a non-main workflow cannot obtain the production deploy credential.

findings.title: Flag and kill-switch changes have no stated authorisation, audit or limit on what a flag may enable
findings.attack_path: A compromised operator session, a support role or a mistaken change flips a feature flag without a deploy: it re-enables a feature the kill switch stopped, switches off a quota reservation or entitlement check, or turns on an AI egress scope, and nothing records who changed it or refuses the change.
findings.recommended_control: Store flags as authorised, audited configuration: every change carries actor, approval and reason and lands in the ADR-020 trail; an absent, malformed or deleted flag or kill-switch row resolves to the safe state (capability disabled, kill engaged) and raises an alert, as ADR-022's kill_switch OFF_AND_ALERT does; a flag never grants an entitlement or bypass a quota, egress or authorisation check; test each refusal.

findings.title: A restore is verified against the ledger only, not against backup integrity or the audit chain
findings.attack_path: An attacker with backup-storage write access, or a silent storage fault, alters or truncates a backup or point-in-time log; the restore drill or a real recovery serves it after the ledger zero-sum check passes, because audit-chain rows and non-ledger tables are never compared with an independent record.
findings.recommended_control: Make backups immutable for their retention (write-once lock), record per-backup checksums outside the backup store, and refuse restore readiness until checksums match and the ADR-020 section 8.5 chain verification against the write-once copy passes; add a planted-corruption restore test.

findings.title: Deploys, rollbacks, IaC applies and flag changes are not attributed to an approving principal
findings.attack_path: A production change, an emergency rollback or a kill-switch flip is made under the single owner account; the published deploy events carry version and duration but no approver or session, so an incident review cannot establish who authorised the change or whether the required approval happened.
findings.recommended_control: Emit every deploy, canary verdict, rollback, IaC apply and flag change as an attributable event carrying the session or workflow identity, the approval reference and the change digest, retained in the in-region security-log stream with synchronised time; test that an unattributed production change fails the pipeline.

findings.title: Traces, span attributes and metric labels from every service reach the collector unfiltered
findings.attack_path: A service records a merchant, amount, e-mail address or provider host as a span attribute or metric label, which api#21's log scrubbing does not cover, or the Python ai-service (ADR-009) logs it without api#21's Kotlin module; the collector forwards it to the trace and metric stores and dashboards, where operators and processors read it outside every access gate.
findings.recommended_control: Enforce a collector-side allowlist of attribute and label keys for traces, metrics and logs from every service, dropping unknown keys and values that match money, contact or host shapes; adopt ADR-022 section 7's label rule; prove it with planted values in each signal type from each service.

findings.title: Hosted server telemetry and paging processors and alert payloads are outside the residency policy
findings.attack_path: Server security logs, traces or error events are exported to a hosted observability service outside India, or an alert template copies log lines and identifiers into a page sent through a third-party paging service, while the residency check covers only stateful resources the pipeline provisions.
findings.recommended_control: Extend the region assertion to every server telemetry and paging destination, permit only processors recorded with a signed agreement under docs#44, keep alert payloads to rule, service and severity with no log excerpt, and fail closed when a destination's region or agreement is unrecorded.

findings.title: A restore from a pre-erasure backup can resurrect an erased user's keys and readable data
findings.attack_path: A user is erased by destroying their key; a later disaster recovery or restore drill restores a backup taken before the erasure, bringing back the wrapped key and blind-index entries, and the environment serves the user's data again before anyone replays the erasure.
findings.recommended_control: Gate restore readiness on replaying the independent erasure tombstone journal to zero outstanding entries, fail closed when the journal is unavailable, and run the erasure harness on the restored dataset; infra#26's restore runbook must call this step rather than document it.

findings.title: Push and e-mail provider copies of recipient addresses and device tokens survive account erasure
findings.attack_path: A user erases their account; api#56 deletes addresses and tokens locally through the erasure path, but the e-mail provider keeps the address in delivery logs and suppression lists and the push provider keeps the token, so the processor retains personal data past erasure with no recorded basis.
findings.recommended_control: Make erasure call each provider's deletion or suppression-removal interface through the provider abstraction, record provider-side retention that cannot be deleted under the docs#44 processor agreements, and test that an erased synthetic recipient is removed or listed with its basis at both providers.

findings.title: No per-recipient or per-class send cap, priority for security messages or provider-throttling handling
findings.attack_path: An event loop, a replayed dead-letter batch or abuse of a user-triggered message class floods the outbox; the provider throttles or suspends the account, spend rises, and security messages such as sign-in alerts queue behind the flood or are dropped while the provider refuses sends.
findings.recommended_control: Cap sends per recipient and per class over a window, throttle dead-letter replay, give security-class messages a reserved lane, treat provider throttling or suspension as an alerting state with failover to the second provider, and prove the caps and the reserved lane with a flood test.

findings.title: A telemetry flood can fill write-once retained log storage and exhaust on-call attention
findings.attack_path: A noisy or hostile client, a failing dependency or a logging bug emits a burst of high-cardinality records; the security-log store, which refuses deletion before expiry, fills irreversibly and costs grow, while repeated alerts page the on-call owner until real pages are ignored.
findings.recommended_control: Bound ingestion per service with rate and cardinality limits and a separate budget for retained security logs, alert on volume and remaining capacity before it is exhausted, and de-duplicate and group alerts; test a synthetic flood against the limits.

findings.title: The identity that applies infrastructure code can rewrite IAM, key policy and retention locks
findings.attack_path: A merged or injected infrastructure change, or a compromised deploy job, edits access policy to grant a human or workload standing data or key access, shortens a retention lock or disables backup immutability; the apply succeeds because the deploy identity holds those permissions and review treats it as routine.
findings.recommended_control: Split the deploy identity from the identity that may change access, key, retention and backup policy; require independent review and a policy-as-code rule that rejects plans weakening those controls; have infra#32's standing-access inventory run after every apply; test a planted grant and a planted lock removal.

findings.title: Host-level access to the self-managed R4 runtime is not in the standing-access inventory
findings.attack_path: An engineer or a compromised automation account holds shell, container-engine or console access to the self-managed hosts ADR-022 selects; it reads application memory, decrypted data in transit or local disks and bypasses the database, object and key broker entirely.
findings.recommended_control: Include host shell, container-engine socket, hypervisor console and host-image access in the standing-access inventory that must be empty, route any host session through the same time-boxed, second-approved, audited broker, and add denial tests for direct host access.

findings.title: The production KEK custodian assigned to T-PLT-03 is not listed in infra#27's scope
findings.attack_path: An attacker who compromises a database host or the hosting account finds the KEK under a file-held software root or as an exportable key beside the data, because no ticket body lists selecting a non-exportable custodian, and unwraps every wrapped user key (baseline T-11).
findings.recommended_control: Record on infra#27 the obligation ADR-018 section 6.1.1 and ADR-022 section 3.3 place on T-PLT-03: select and prove an India-resident, non-exportable custodian administratively separate from the database hosts and backups, with every unwrap logged to alerting, and keep real data refused until it passes.

findings.title: The AI workload could be deployed before the ADR-022 runtime gates pass, with keys readable by the deploy identity
findings.attack_path: The runtime is provisioned and the AI gateway deployed because the pipeline is green, while startup denial, nftables ordering or kill-switch evidence is unproven, or the deploy identity can read provider keys from the secret store; a compromised gateway or pipeline then reaches providers or private addresses directly.
findings.recommended_control: Make the deployment gate refuse the AI workload until the T7, T12, T19 and T20 evidence of adr/ai-egress-consequences.json is present for the exact digest, keep provider keys readable only by the gateway runtime identity, and test that a missing gate result blocks the deploy.

findings.title: The sessionless unsubscribe reference is not required to be unguessable or to need a confirming request
findings.attack_path: An e-mail security scanner prefetches every link and withdraws consent on GET, or an attacker enumerates or replays references and unsubscribes a victim from security-class or chosen messages, silencing alerts without a session.
findings.recommended_control: Issue unsubscribe references as high-entropy, recipient- and class-bound, revocable values; make the withdrawal a confirming POST rather than a GET side effect; rate-limit and alert on failed lookups; keep security classes unsubscribable only through the authenticated editors; test prefetch, guess and replay.

findings.title: Provider delivery callbacks are mapped but not authenticated or replay-checked
findings.attack_path: Anyone who learns the callback route posts forged bounce, complaint or delivered statuses; a forged bounce suppresses a user's channel, a forged delivered status hides a failing provider, and replays skew the dashboard.
findings.recommended_control: Verify each callback's provider signature or authenticated channel and freshness before mapping, process idempotently on the provider event identifier, record and rate-limit rejected attempts without secrets, and test forged, stale and replayed callbacks.

findings.title: Play Console account hardening, user roster and the upload-key reset path are not covered
findings.attack_path: An attacker phishes the Play Console developer account or a user it added, requests an upload-key reset or uploads with a new key, and promotes a malicious build past the tracks; the bundle is signed by Play App Signing and installs as a trusted update on every device.
findings.recommended_control: Record the Play Console user roster with least-privilege roles, phishing-resistant sign-in on every member, alerting on user and key changes, the upload-key reset as an owner-only recovery step, and promotion permission separated from upload; verify it with read-only evidence per release.

findings.title: Human access to the push, e-mail and paging or uptime vendor consoles is ungoverned
findings.attack_path: A holder of the e-mail or push provider console, or a stale former member, reads recipient addresses and delivery history or changes sender settings; a holder of the paging console silences or reroutes pages during an incident. infra#43 concerned only the GitHub identity and was closed with hardening deferred, api#59 the ADR-020 administrative identity domain, and api#56 and infra#27 API credentials and the log store; none covered these vendor console accounts, and infra#93 now owns their governance.
findings.recommended_control: Create an owning ticket for third-party operational console accounts: roster, least-privilege roles, phishing-resistant sign-in, joiner and leaver revocation, audit export and a revocation drill per service, recorded before any real recipient or page flows through them.

findings.title: The hosting-account owner and the domain registrar and DNS account identities are not hardened
findings.attack_path: An attacker who phishes or recovers the hosting-account owner credential snapshots disks, deletes hosts, backups and the secondary-region copies or grants itself host and custodian access; an attacker holding the registrar or DNS account repoints the origin. Neither identity is in infra#32's standing-grant inventory, infra#43 concerned only GitHub, and no existing ticket covered them; infra#94 now owns their hardening.
findings.recommended_control: Create an owning ticket for infrastructure owner identities: phishing-resistant sign-in, offline break-glass custody, no daily use, alerting on owner and registrar actions, and backups and the key custodian kept beyond that account's unilateral deletion (separate account or retention lock); rehearse recovery.

findings.title: The public origin is uncontrolled: registrar and DNS records, certificate issuance, TLS key custody and RP ID file hosting
findings.attack_path: An attacker who takes the registrar or DNS account, obtains a certificate for the domain or copies a host's TLS private key serves the genuine origin, relays passkey assertions or alters the assetlinks and webauthn files on the RP ID apex; app links and passkeys then trust the attacker, and a wrong RP ID cannot be repaired once credentials exist.
findings.recommended_control: Create an owner for the public origin: DNS records and certificate authority authorisation as reviewed code, certificate issuance monitored, TLS private keys generated on and confined to the ingress hosts with rotation, RP ID files served only by the production pipeline, and pin rotation coordinated with android#27.

findings.title: No edge request capacity, per-address and per-route limits or flood protection for the self-managed ingress
findings.attack_path: A request flood or slow-connection attack from many addresses reaches the R4 hosts directly, because ADR-022 provides no managed edge and only authentication and sensitive operations are rate limited (api#40); the hosts exhaust connections and CPU and every service, including security messages and restores, becomes unavailable.
findings.recommended_control: Assign the ingress capacity plan to an owner: per-address and per-route limits, connection and body-size bounds, an upstream flood-absorption option recorded with its processor terms, and an alert before saturation; test a synthetic flood against the limits.

findings.title: Host OS, kernel, Docker Engine, runc and nftables patching on the R4 hosts has no cadence, scan or re-qualification
findings.attack_path: A known kernel, Docker Engine or runc vulnerability stays unpatched on a self-managed R4 host; a compromised workload, such as the AI service handling hostile input, escapes its container to the host and bypasses the namespaces, nftables rules and broker that ADR-022 relies on, reaching keys and data of every service.
findings.recommended_control: Under infra#25's container runtime provisioning and rebuild-from-code scope (ADR-022 section 3.3, T-PLT-01): publish a patch cadence and an emergency CVE response time, rebuild hosts from code, scan host images for vulnerabilities and drift, and re-run the ADR-022 runtime gates before admission after every patch.

findings.title: Retained security logs have no authenticated time source and no emitter authentication at the collector
findings.attack_path: An attacker on the network path shifts the hosts' time source, or a compromised service or client writes into the collector as another emitter; entries carry false times or forged origins, drift alerting stays quiet because it compares against the shifted source, and append-only retention preserves the forgeries as CERT-In evidence.
findings.recommended_control: Within infra#27's clock-synchronisation, collector and retention scope: use authenticated time sources cross-checked against a second source, authenticate every emitter to the collector with workload identity, keep client telemetry out of the security-log stream, accept structured fields only, and test a shifted source and an unauthenticated emitter.

findings.title: The upload key and Play publishing credential are not confined to the protected Android release workflow
findings.attack_path: A workflow on a feature branch or pull request in the Android repository, such as one an automated session pushes, obtains the upload key or the Play publishing credential, signs a malicious bundle and uploads it to a track; Play App Signing re-signs it and it installs as a trusted update.
findings.recommended_control: Under android#37's upload-key custody and rotation scope: release the upload key and Play publishing credential only to the protected release workflow on main with a named environment and required approval, refuse pull-request and branch contexts with a negative test, and record an upload-key rotation drill.

findings.title: A restore silently rewinds usage-ledger, purchase and settlement events inside the recovery-point window
findings.attack_path: After a restore to the recovery point, usage reservations, purchase or refund events and split settlements recorded after it are gone while the ledger stays internally consistent; the zero-sum check passes, a user regains spent quota or loses a paid entitlement, and a settled share reappears as owed.
findings.recommended_control: Within infra#26's restore drill and sample reconciliation: reconcile restored usage, purchase and settlement events against an independent record (the ADR-020 audit chain and its write-once copy, store receipts), list every event lost inside the recovery-point window for replay or user notice, and test it with events planted after the recovery point.
